rv.q: Full of energy and passion, every wonderfully radiant minute in Jaja’s salon is something to savour.
You’d be hard-pressed to see anything else quite this alive and energised in the theatre.
When the play finishes – as if mid-sentence, just as word of a drama involving ICE agents reaches the salon – it feels all too soon.
It is gloriously performed, with heart and masses of character, and directed exuberantly by the talented Touko.
For all its flaws though, Jaja’s African Hair Braiding vividly sketches in unseen lives.

Still, until then the good vibes hold your attention in Jaja’s African Hair Braiding, a play, first staged at the Manhattan Theatre Club in 2023, which offers an exuberant glimpse of West African immigrants building new lives.
Our world at large may be unravelling, but this play’s intricate weave, for the most part, is just right.
For most of its 90 minutes, though, it’s a fast-talking joy.
Nonetheless, Bioh has a talent for creating authentic and culturally specific stories that resonate with all audiences.
It would be hard to not fall for the charm of Jaja’s African Hair Braiding.
